summary: Pointed to Jesus by John the Baptist, Andrew and another disciple follow Him; then Simon, Philip and Nathanael come, and Jesus promises them greater things.
key_insight: Jesus answered the first two disciples with “Come and see.” A day later, when Nathanael scoffed at Nazareth, Philip did not argue; he used Jesus’ own words: “Come and see.” From the first day, those who found Jesus went to find someone else.
story: The next day John the Baptist was standing with two of his disciples. Seeing Jesus walking by, he said, “Behold the Lamb of God!” The two disciples heard him, and they followed Jesus.

Jesus turned and saw them following. “What do you seek?” He asked. They called Him “Rabbi” and asked, “where are You staying?” He said, “Come and see.” So they came and saw where He was staying and remained with Him that day. It was about the tenth hour.

One of the two was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. The first thing he did was find his own brother Simon and tell him, “We have found the Messiah.” He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas,” which means “A Stone.”

The following day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip, who came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter, and said to him, “Follow Me.” Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found Him of whom Moses in the law, and also the prophets, wrote,” and named Him: “Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” Nathanael answered, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said, “Come and see.”

As Nathanael came toward Him, Jesus said, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!” “How do You know me?” Nathanael asked. Jesus answered, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael said, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”

Jesus answered, “You will see greater things than these.” And He added, “Most assuredly, I say to you, hereafter you shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

fit.question: John says Andrew, Simon and others began following Jesus near the Jordan. Matthew, Mark and Luke say Jesus called Simon, Andrew, James and John beside the Sea of Galilee, and they left their nets. Which was the first call?

points.label: A first meeting, then a call
points.text: John describes the first meeting and the first stirrings of faith. Some time later, back in Galilee, Jesus called these men to leave their work and follow Him for good (Mark 1:16–20). In between, they seem to have returned to fishing.

points.label: Why they left their nets so quickly
points.text: The call by the sea makes more sense because of this earlier meeting. When Jesus said, “Follow Me,” the fishermen already knew Him, had heard John’s witness, and had seen the sign at Cana (John 2:11).

fit.note: The accounts describe different stages in the same men’s journey to Jesus, and each fills in what the other leaves out.
fit.short: John tells of the first meeting near the Jordan; the other Gospels tell of the later call by the sea to leave everything.

scene.label: “The Lamb of God”
scene.text: John the Baptist had said it the day before, adding “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Every Jew knew the Passover lamb and the lambs offered daily at the temple, and Isaiah had pictured God’s Servant “led as a lamb to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7).

scene.label: The tenth hour
scene.text: Counting hours from sunrise, as people usually did, this was about four in the afternoon. With the day nearly over, the two probably stayed the night.

scene.label: The unnamed disciple
scene.text: John’s Gospel never names the second of the two. Many believe it was John the son of Zebedee, the writer himself, who never uses his own name in his Gospel.

scene.label: Nathanael
scene.text: He came from Cana in Galilee (John 21:2). His name does not appear in the lists of the Twelve, but many identify him with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in those lists (Matthew 10:3). Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a prophet’s picture of peace (Micah 4:4); what Nathanael was doing there, John does not say.

scene.label: Jacob’s ladder
scene.text: Jesus’ last words echo Jacob’s dream, where “the angels of God were ascending and descending” on a ladder to heaven (Genesis 28:12). Jacob was the man of deceit (Genesis 27:35); Nathanael is an Israelite “in whom is no deceit.” Jesus Himself is now the place where heaven meets earth.

witnesses.john: John alone tells how the first disciples met Jesus, with the small details of an eyewitness: the hour of the day, the words of each exchange. In these few verses Jesus is called the Lamb of God, Rabbi, the Messiah, the One Moses wrote about, the Son of God, the King of Israel, and the Son of Man. John’s Gospel was written so that readers would believe (20:31), and here the first believers meet Him.

seeing.reveals: Jesus knows people before they come to Him. He sees Simon and names his future, and He saw Nathanael under the fig tree. He is the Son of Man on whom heaven opens.
seeing.living: Andrew and Philip did not argue anyone into faith. They told what they had found and brought people to Jesus. When Nathanael scoffed, Philip simply said, “Come and see.” Bring honest doubters to Jesus Himself, and let Him do what only He can.
seeing.ponder: Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel are a question: “What do you seek?” What would your honest answer be today?

preaching.big_idea: Those who find Jesus bring others to come and see Him for themselves.
preaching.watch_for: John counts the days carefully from 1:19 to 2:1 (“the next day” in 1:29, 35 and 43; “the third day” in 2:1). Some see a week of new beginnings in a Gospel that opens “In the beginning” (1:1); at the least, these days were remembered in detail.
